talks.title: KYC and XMR FOR HACKERS
talks.teaser: Shows how technologists can use Monero to pay for goods and services without KYC checks, and which correlation attacks and mitigations matter.
talks.summary:
The talk is a practical tour of using Monero (XMR) to buy goods and services without handing identity documents to an exchange. The speaker stresses that it is not trading advice and that each listener must judge their own threat model, since no single operational security approach fits everyone. Bitcoin serves as the contrast throughout: its public ledger can expose purchases long after the fact, and fraud-scoring tools can flag coins that touched mixers, which makes ordinary payments risky.

Using a worked example of a collectible card sale, the speaker shows how Monero's private-by-default design avoids that exposure. Getting XMR still usually means passing through an exchange that collects identity data. The main threats to Monero users are timing correlation, poisoned nodes that log transactions, and dust attacks that tag wallets. Suggested defenses include routing traffic through Tor, running your own node, blacklisting dusted addresses, using one-time addresses, and holding funds before spending them.

The talk closes with places to spend XMR, such as privacy-focused hosting and VPN providers, and wallet options including Cake Wallet and the official desktop wallet. Decentralized exchanges and the free book Mastering Monero are offered as starting points. The takeaway is that the chain's underlying math has not been publicly broken, so most failures come from user mistakes.

talks.title: The C-m Stained Precipice of Digital Redlining
talks.teaser: Shows how a Springfield, Massachusetts nonprofit turns discarded laptops into Linux learning machines to counter digital redlining.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the rising cost of new laptops and the gap in device access that follows. The speakers describe Springfield, Massachusetts, where many residents rely on a smartphone as their only device, and argue that school and government programs often hand out restricted, loaner-only machines that teach people to use commercial products rather than understand them.

The middle of the talk covers their grassroots nonprofit, which takes donated and discarded hardware, repairs it, and installs Linux, including Fedora on low-end Chromebooks. Their classes explain how boot loaders and video output work, and students keep the computers they build. The speakers also describe obstacles: state surplus rules that charge for equipment, and donors who hand over laptops without RAM or drives, leaving them unusable.

The closing section asks for donations to cover batteries, screens, keyboards and memory. The speakers report that students who once saw no future in technology began considering teaching or web development after hands-on open-source classes. The practical takeaway is that giving people modifiable hardware and a foundation in how it works can counter the throwaway cycle of consumer tech.

talks.title: The Enshittified Internet & How We Can Rewild the Internet
talks.teaser: Surveys how the web became dominated by big-tech platforms and offers self-hosting and decentralized alternatives for reclaiming online services.
talks.summary:
The talk traces the internet's history from early academic networks and bulletin boards through Usenet, IRC and the first walled gardens such as CompuServe and AOL. The speaker then follows the shift to browser bundling, ad-funded search and social platforms, and the rise of AI-generated content. The decline is framed as a result of corporate greed and surveillance, and the speaker links it to proposed age verification and online safety laws.

The middle of the talk is a practical list of replacements for mainstream services. Suggestions include privacy-focused browsers, a search option with AI answers switched off, encrypted notes and email providers, OpenStreetMap for maps, and Codeberg or Sourcehut for code hosting. For video and files, the speaker recommends a self-hosted Jellyfin server, Nextcloud, and a Raspberry Pi media box. The speaker also covers fediverse services such as Mastodon, PixelFed and PeerTube, pre-built self-hosting distributions, and Valid, a decentralized network presented as a node-based alternative to Tor-style routing. Offline sharing with a PirateBox-style device is also mentioned.

The closing argument is that older protocols such as Gopher, IRC, BBS and Usenet still work and can be run again. The speaker urges experienced members of the community to teach younger hackers how to run these services, and frames reclaiming the web as a collective effort rather than an individual one.
